# Collaboration with Git {#sec-git}

Git keeps a project's history as a chain of **commits**. Each commit records a snapshot,
its author and a message. A useful history lets a teammate understand a change, find a
regression, undo a mistake or bring a fix to an older release.

This chapter is not a Git course. It explains the decisions a team makes around that
history: what belongs in a commit, how changes reach the shared branch and how a fix reaches
users of an older version.

## One change per commit {#sec-atomic-commits}

Suppose you fix a crash when opening an empty sketch and also change the canvas colors. Both
changes work, but they solve different problems. Put them in separate commits: the crash fix
can then be reviewed, reverted or copied to an older release without taking the colors with it.

That is an **atomic commit**: one self-contained change. Include its tests and any necessary
supporting changes, and aim to keep the project building and the tests passing at that point
in history. A large feature can be several such steps; atomic does not mean one file or one
line.

Git records what you **stage**, not every edit in your working directory. Inspect that
selection before you commit:

```sh
git add -p          # choose changes in small pieces
git diff --cached   # review the staged result
git commit
```

On a shared branch, undo a change with a new commit instead of rewriting history. For example,
`git revert --no-commit <commit>` applies the inverse change so you can inspect it and write
a `revert:` message explaining why.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Recording changes to the repository](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Recording-Changes-to-the-Repository)
:::

## Keep large media out of history {#sec-large-media}

Git retains committed files in history, including old versions after you delete or replace
them. For large images or videos used in a README, consider hosting them outside the
repository and linking to them. On GitHub, you can upload an image to an issue or pull
request comment and use the resulting attachment URL. Keep a copy under your control and
check that the link remains accessible to your readers. For large files the project must
version, consider [Git LFS](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/about-git-large-file-storage).

## A message for the next reader {#sec-commit-messages}

The diff shows *what* changed. The commit message gives a future reader the reason and the
context that the code cannot show. Start with a short summary, leave a blank line, then explain
why the change was needed. Finish with optional metadata, such as an issue reference.

This template uses [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/):
a type before the summary tells both people and tools what kind of change it is. An optional
scope names the affected area.

```{.default filename="Commit message"}
fix(sketchbook): prevent a crash when opening an empty sketch

An empty file has no strokes to load. Treat it as an empty sketch so
users can open it instead of losing access to their work.

Closes: #42
```

Here `fix` says this is a bug fix and `sketchbook` names the area. `Closes: #42` is a
**trailer**, a labelled piece of metadata at the end of the message. Other examples include
`Co-authored-by:` and links to a review.

| Type | A change that ... |
|---|---|
| `feat` | adds a feature |
| `fix` | fixes a bug |
| `docs`, `test`, `style` | changes documentation, tests or formatting |
| `refactor`, `perf` | restructures code or improves performance |
| `build`, `ci`, `chore` | changes the build, automation or project maintenance |
| `revert` | undoes an earlier change |

Use a short, lower-case imperative summary, such as “add” rather than “added”. This template
requires a body, limits the subject and body prose to 72 characters per line, and omits the
subject's final period. Conventional Commits itself leaves the body optional and does not set
those limits: they are this template's choices, checked by its hooks.

Other teams use a plain imperative subject, such as `Prevent a crash on empty sketches`, or
their own prefixes. The important part is a shared convention. Conventional Commits adds a
benefit: release tools can recognize `fix`, `feat` and breaking changes when preparing a
changelog or suggesting a version. The team still reviews the result.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/),
[Git trailers](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-interpret-trailers)
:::

## Tell users when a change breaks compatibility {#sec-breaking-changes}

Imagine an app exposes a REST endpoint used by another program. Removing that endpoint may
leave the app itself working, but the other program breaks when it upgrades. That is a
**breaking change**: it changes a contract existing users depend on.

Conventional Commits offers two ways to flag it. Put `!` before the colon in the subject:

```{.default filename="Breaking change in the subject"}
feat(api)!: remove v1 REST endpoints

Clients must use v2 before upgrading.
```

Or add a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer that describes the impact:

```{.default filename="Breaking change in a footer"}
feat(api): remove v1 REST endpoints

Clients must use v2 before upgrading.

BREAKING CHANGE: The v1 REST endpoints no longer accept requests.
```

Both mark the commit as breaking; a footer also gives release tools an explicit description.
Neither form changes the version by itself. A release pipeline must be configured to act on
the marker, and a reviewer must decide whether the change is actually incompatible.

Some projects add a `[ChangeLog]` marker to selected messages to identify changes for release
notes. That is a separate project convention, not part of Conventional Commits. Use it when
your chosen changelog tool understands it; users generally need to hear about the effect of a
change, not every internal commit.

## Hooks: feedback before a commit {#sec-git-hooks}

A **hook** is a program Git runs at a particular point in a command. The template's hooks
check the staged C++ and QML formatting and whitespace, then check the commit message. They
also warn about staged files over 50 KB without blocking the commit. They report problems
without changing your files. They cannot judge whether the explanation is useful or replace a
build and tests.

Git does not enable hooks from a cloned repository automatically. Once you have initialized
your project from the template, enable these hooks in each clone:

```sh
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

This replaces any existing hook path for that clone. The checks need `clang-format` for C++
and Qt's `qmlformat` for QML. If a check fails, fix the file or message and try again. The
`format` target formats the working files; stage the intended result afterwards.

Local hooks can be bypassed, so the template also checks commit messages in GitHub Actions.
For a shared repository, require the `commits` status check and pull requests for `main` in
[branch protection](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches).
Keep build and test checks there too.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `.githooks/`, `tools/check_commit_message.sh`, `.github/workflows/git-policy.yml`

**Read more:** [Git hooks](https://git-scm.com/docs/githooks)
:::

## Bringing work together {#sec-trunk-based-development}

A **branch** is a movable name for a commit. When you start a feature branch, it shares the
history of `main`. While you work, someone else may add a commit to `main`:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C<br/>main))
    B --> D((D)) --> E((E<br/>feature))
```

Read the arrows as “followed by”. `C` is the new work on `main`; `D` and `E` are the feature
commits. There are two common ways to combine them:

**Merge** joins both histories. A merge commit `M` has two parents, so the history records
where the branches came together. The existing commits keep their identities.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> M((M<br/>main))
    B --> D((D)) --> E((E)) --> M
```

**Rebase** reapplies the feature commits after `C`. Git creates new commits `D′` and `E′`
with the same intended changes but new identities: their parent has changed. Once the branch
is reviewed, a fast-forward merge moves `main` to `E′`, giving a linear history.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> D((D′)) --> E((E′<br/>main))
```

Rebase preserves the individual changes and their messages, not their original commit IDs.
Resolve conflicts and test again: replaying a change onto a newer base can change its result.
Rebase your own short-lived branch before it joins `main`; do not rewrite shared history that
others already depend on.

The template favors **trunk-based development**: the team integrates small, reviewed changes
into `main` frequently and keeps it releasable. Short-lived branches make review possible
without letting work drift apart for weeks. A practical sequence is:

```sh
git switch -c feat/pressure-strokes
# make and test small commits
git push -u origin feat/pressure-strokes
# open a pull request; after main moves on:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease
```

`--force-with-lease` updates your published branch after a rebase only if the remote still
matches what you expect. Coordinate before rewriting a branch someone else uses. After review
and passing checks, a rebase merge can put the individual commits on `main` in a straight
line. A squash merge instead combines the branch changes into one new commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Fix an earlier commit
During review you may find a mistake in an earlier commit on your branch. The optional
[git-revise](https://git-revise.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) tool folds a staged correction
into that commit and updates the commits after it:

```sh
git add path/to/corrected-file
git revise <commit>
```

This rewrites the affected commits, so use it on your own branch before integration and
coordinate with anyone sharing that branch. Recheck the changes and tests afterwards. Git's
built-in interactive rebase and fixup commits can do the same job without an extra tool.
:::

Other teams make different trade-offs. [GitHub Flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow)
uses short-lived branches and pull requests. [Git Flow](https://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/)
also has long-lived development and release branches, which can help with scheduled releases
but need more coordination. Pick a workflow for the team's release needs.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Trunk-Based Development](https://trunkbaseddevelopment.com/),
[Git branching and merging](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging),
[Git rebase](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase)
:::

## Versions, releases and backports {#sec-versions-and-backports}

A **version** tells a user which release they have. With
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html), a version has three numbers:

| Change | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Patch | `1.2.0` → `1.2.1` | a backward-compatible bug fix |
| Minor | `1.2.1` → `1.3.0` | backward-compatible functionality |
| Major | `1.3.0` → `2.0.0` | an incompatible public change |

These promises need a defined public contract: for an app that might include a file format,
an API or commands used by scripts. Before `1.0.0`, SemVer treats the public API as unstable.
A **tag** such as `v1.2.0` names the exact commit used for a release; a branch can continue
moving as more fixes are added.

Now imagine users run both version `1.2` and the newer `2.2`. You discover a serious bug in
both. Fix and test it on `main` for the next release, then bring the same fix to the
`release/1.2` maintenance branch. That branch starts at the old release and contains only
the fixes the team chooses to support there. Test the backport and release `1.2.1`, tagged
at its own commit. Users can receive the fix without upgrading to version 2.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    A["v1.2.0<br/>released"] --> B["v2.2.0<br/>released"] --> C["Fix on main"]
    A --> D["release/1.2<br/>maintenance"] --> E["Backport fix<br/>tag v1.2.1"]
    C -. "copy the fix" .-> E
```

Copying a commit to another branch is called **cherry-picking** or **backporting**. An atomic
fix is easier to pick because it brings the fix and its test without unrelated features:

```sh
git switch release/1.2
git cherry-pick -x <fix-commit>
```

The result is a new commit on the maintenance branch. The `-x` option records the original
commit when the pick applies without conflicts; after resolving a conflict, check the message
and add that reference if needed. A fix may need adaptation if version 1 has different code.
Maintain older branches only for releases you have chosen to support.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `CMakeLists.txt` sets the app version; the release build puts it in the package

**Read more:** [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html),
[Git tags](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging),
[Git cherry-pick](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-cherry-pick)
:::
